lines.text: Every ninety seconds, an aircraft lands in San Francisco.
Hundreds of people on board. Thousands of feet up. And every one of them is waiting for a voice.
San Francisco Tower, Starlux twelve, ten mile final, runway two eight right.
Starlux twelve, San Francisco Tower, wind two eight zero at twelve, runway two eight right, cleared to land.
Three seats. Three ways to run the sky. Pick one.
Mission one. A Lufthansa seven-four-seven sits nose-in at gate A eight, bound for Frankfurt. But a jumbo can't drive backwards. Give the word, and the tug swings it out.
From above, the airport is a maze of lettered roads. You call the route, one taxiway at a time, and watch each one light up.
Down here, things move fast. Sometimes the safest thing you can say is: stop. Hold it. Then let it go.
This is the big one. Between this jet and its runway lies another runway. And someone is taking off on it. Nobody crosses without your word.
Two jets. One taxiway. Rolling straight at each other. Decide who goes first, before they decide for you.
The runway belongs to the tower. Your last job on the ground: hand it over, clean.
Welcome to the tower. One sentence from you sends seventy tons of metal down the runway at a hundred and sixty knots. Make it count.
An Airbus is seven miles out, riding the glide path down. It needs three words from you before its wheels touch the ground.
At San Francisco, the runways cross. A departure and an arrival, aiming for the same patch of concrete. Timing is everything.
There's a Cessna sitting on the runway. And a jet, two miles out, coming in fast. You have seconds.
This is the approach radar. Every blip is a plane full of people. You move them with three numbers: heading, altitude, speed.
Somewhere out there is an invisible beam that leads to the runway. Point the jet at it, gently. Get it right, and it flies itself home.
Two jets. Same altitude. Closing fast. Three miles apart, or a thousand feet. Keep them there.
Now watch the tug swing it out.
Clear it to the runway. Name the taxiways.
Stop it, right where it is.
Good. Now let it roll again.
Wait. Let the departure go first.
Line it up on the runway.
Arrival first. Clear it to land.
Hold the departure. Let the arrival pass.
Before your first call, learn to talk like a controller. Three rules. That's all it takes.
Callsigns. Say the airline's radio name, then the flight number. D L H four five five is Lufthansa four fifty-five.
Numbers. Runways and headings, digit by digit. Altitudes in thousands. Zero one right. Heading two seven zero. Five thousand.
Letters use the phonetic alphabet. M five is Mike five. A one is Alpha one.
That's the language. Now let's move a jumbo jet.
Turn left heading two seven zero.
Climb and maintain one one thousand.
Reduce speed to two one zero knots.
Contact tower one one eight point five.
Taxi via Mike five, Mike one, Alpha two.
